newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bills close weaker as NZ dollar falls sharply.
newsitem.headline: Bills close weaker as NZ dollar falls sharply.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
90-DAY BILLS (MAR) 92.83 (PREV 92.88) 90-DAYS 7.40 (PREV 7.38)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.45 PCT (PREV 7.55) US 5-YR 6.31 (PREV 6.29)
* Bank bills, short bonds sold off as currency slides
* Longer end encouraged by speech by RB's Brash
* Market watching TWI for direction
New Zealand bank bills and short bond yields closed higher in response to a sharply lower New Zealand dollar after a choppy session on Thursday.
However, the long end closed reasonably well bid after they took encouragement from a speech by Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash who said the bank would not go soft on inflation.
Despite the dollar's three quarters of a cent fall, the Trade-Weighted Index held reasonable firm, limiting weakness in the short-end.
Bill dealers said they will be watching the TWI closely for signs of weakness and direction.
"I'd be tempted to say the downside will suffer if we see any more weakness in the TWI," said a Wellington dealer.
Some players had been expecting Brash to comment more directly on interest rates -- that the rally since September had gone far enough -- and the failure to comment prompted weakness in the currency.
Westpac Bank's head of financial markets, Chris Rand said there was little new in Brash's speech.
"He obviously doesn't like the current mix of policy but really there was nothing new there.
"There was nothing for the markets to get excited about...and certainly there was nothing there for the exporters to point at to say that there could be some respite coming for them."
There was interest in Brash's comments about unrealistic growth expectations which appeared to be directed at Treasurer Winston Peters, Rand said.

Brash said potential sustainable annual growth was around 3.0 percent. Peters NZ First's economic policy for last year's election set a target of six percent GDP growth by the end of its first term in government.
"I think he (Brash) is basically saying that those are unrealistic given what's expected to happen over the next two to three years," Rand said.
September quarter GDP data was slightly stronger than economists' forecasts but markets took little note, saying the information gave mixed messages.
Dealers said the numbers were more supportive of Treasury's view of stronger growth in the economy than the Reserve Bank's but that may be bearish for inflation and monetary policy.
"The economics on the day should have pointed towards a resilient currency but it failed on technicals," said Bankers Trust's John MacFarlane.
